claims.text: Algorithmic machine learning models can produce unfair decisions by reproducing biases present in historical training data.
Legal, institutional, or commercial constraints can prevent organizations from collecting or holding sensitive attribute data needed to detect indirect discrimination.
Organizations often lack the knowledge and capacity required to identify emergent fairness issues in complex sociotechnical systems.
Trusted third parties can selectively store sensitive data in a privacy-preserving manner to perform discrimination discovery and fairness model constraints.
Collaborative online platforms enable organizations to share contextual and experiential knowledge to improve fairness in machine learning.
Unsupervised learning and pedagogically interpretable algorithms can enable the generation of fairness hypotheses for selective testing.
Real-world machine learning fairness challenges are institutionally and contextually grounded rather than abstract constrained optimization problems.

evidence.description: Decisions based on algorithmic, machine learning models can be unfair, reproducing biases in historical data used to train them.

For legal, institutional or commercial reasons, organisations might not hold the data on sensitive attributes such as gender, ethnicity, sexuality or disability needed to diagnose and mitigate emergent indirect discrimination-by-proxy, such as redlining.
Such organisations might also lack the knowledge and capacity to identify and manage fairness issues that are emergent properties of complex sociotechnical systems.
Trusted third parties could selectively store data necessary for performing discrimination discovery and incorporating fairness constraints into model-building in a privacy-preserving manner.
Collaborative online platforms would allow diverse organisations to record, share and access contextual and experiential knowledge to promote fairness in machine learning systems.
Unsupervised learning and pedagogically interpretable algorithms might allow fairness hypotheses to be built for further selective testing and exploration.
Real-world fairness challenges in machine learning are not abstract, constrained optimisation problems, but are institutionally and contextually grounded.

methodologies.name: Privacy-Preserving Trusted Third Party Architecture
methodologies.description: Utilizing trusted third parties to store sensitive attribute data selectively and enable discrimination discovery without direct organization access.
conditions: Organizations lacking sensitive data due to legal or institutional limits

methodologies.name: Collaborative Knowledge-Sharing Platforms
methodologies.description: Online platforms enabling diverse institutions to record and share experiential and contextual fairness insights.
conditions: Complex sociotechnical machine learning deployment contexts

methodologies.name: Exploratory Fairness Discovery via Unsupervised and Interpretable Learning
methodologies.description: Applying unsupervised methods and interpretable models to formulate and selectively test fairness hypotheses.

limitations.text: Organisations often do not hold sensitive demographic data required to diagnose and mitigate indirect discrimination-by-proxy due to legal, institutional, or commercial constraints.
Existing machine learning fairness tools are often designed as abstract constrained optimization problems, failing to address messy institutional and deployment contexts.

future_work.text: Research and develop computational fairness tools directly within and alongside the messy institutional contexts that shape their actual deployment.
